sections.history: Elumiyankottur, a village near Perambakkam in the Thondai country north-west of Chennai, holds an old Shiva shrine praised in the Tevaram, which marks it a Paadal Petra Sthalam. The place carries older names in tradition—Rambaikottur, then Elambayankottur—from which the present Elumiyankottur has come. Tradition holds that Rambha, foremost of the celestial dancers, performed long penance before the Lord here and was granted the boon of unfading youth and beauty, so that the Lord came to be called Arambeswarar, and the village Rambaikottur. The Lord is worshipped as Deivanatheswarar, with the goddess Kanakakujambikai. The child-saint Tirugnanasambandar is remembered as having sung the temple's decad, and one account tells that Shiva appeared to him here in the guise of an aged man and bade him raise his voice in praise. Raised in stone and kept in worship across the centuries, the shrine remains a quiet sanctuary of the Thondai plain.
sections.architecture: The temple follows the plan of an old village Shiva shrine of the Thondai country. The sanctum holds the linga of Deivanatheswarar, and the goddess Kanakakujambikai is honoured in her own shrine. The jasmine—mullai—is cherished as the sthala vriksham, the temple's sacred tree, and the temple tank is known as the Mallika Pushkarini, the pool of jasmine. Among the daily observances the cow puja is kept here with particular devotion. The enclosure, with its gateway and the tower above the sanctum, carries the simple dignity of a rural Tevaram shrine rather than the grand scale of the great city temples.
sections.legends: Two memories are woven into the temple. The first is of Rambha, the foremost of the heavenly dancers, who is said to have come here and done long penance before the Lord, seeking the gift of youth and beauty that would never fade; pleased with her devotion, the Lord granted the boon and took the name Arambeswarar, from which the village was long called Rambaikottur. The second is the memory, shared with other shrines of this country, of the Tripura Samhara—Shiva's destruction with a single arrow of the three flying cities of the asuras, built of gold, silver and iron. Tradition adds that the Lord appeared at this place to the child-saint Tirugnanasambandar in the form of an aged man and commanded him to sing, and the decad that followed set the temple among the Paadal Petra Sthalams.
sections.festivals: As at every Shiva temple, Maha Shivaratri is kept with night-long worship, the monthly Pradosham is observed, and the sacred days of the Tamil month are marked with special pujas; the cow puja is a cherished part of the temple's routine. A village temple of this kind keeps its own annual festival calendar by the Tamil almanac, so confirm the dates locally before planning a visit.
sections.experience: Elumiyankottur offers the quiet of a country shrine away from the pilgrim crowds. Come to the Lord Deivanatheswarar in the sanctum and to the goddess Kanakakujambikai in her shrine, pause by the jasmine that is the temple's sacred tree and the Mallika Pushkarini tank, and take in the unhurried rhythm of a village that has kept worship here across many names and many centuries. Those who know the story of Rambha come seeking the Lord's grace for health and renewal, and the surrounding fields of the Thondai country lend the place a deep stillness.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Elumiyankottur lies near Perambakkam in Tiruvallur district, in the country west of Chennai and not far from Koovam. Buses reach the area from Tiruvallur and the neighbouring towns, and Tiruvallur, on the Chennai suburban railway, is the convenient rail point; a local vehicle covers the last stretch to the village. Confirm the route locally before setting out, as the temple stands off the main roads.
